parts.title: A week without my phone
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When my mother told me that I could not use my phone for a week, I thought it was a terrible joke. I am fifteen, and I use my phone for everything: talking to friends, listening to music, and even waking up in the morning.

On the first day, I kept reaching for my pocket every few minutes. By the evening, I felt strangely lost. I did not know what was happening in my friends' lives, and I imagined that everyone was talking about me. I almost gave up.

But on the third day, something changed. I read an entire book for the first time in months, and I went for a long walk with my dog without checking any messages. At dinner, my parents and I talked for an hour about nothing in particular, and I realised how much I had missed it.

When the week ended, I was surprised that I did not run to my phone. I switched it on, answered the important messages, and then left it on the kitchen table. I still use it every day, but now I turn it off at ten o'clock, and I sleep much better.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel about his mother's decision?
options: He thought it was a joke
He was glad to have a rest
He agreed to it at once
questions.explanation: He thought it was a terrible joke.

questions.prompt: How did he feel on the first evening?
questions.explanation: By the evening he felt strangely lost and imagined that everyone was talking about him.

questions.prompt: What happened on the third day?
options: He visited a group of friends

He used his phone in secret
questions.explanation: He read a whole book and went for a long walk with his dog.

questions.prompt: What did he realise at dinner?
options: His parents were angry with him
questions.explanation: He talked with his parents for an hour and realised how much he had missed it.

questions.prompt: What does he do now?
options: Never uses a phone any more
Switches off his phone at night
questions.explanation: He now turns his phone off at ten o'clock.

parts.title: How to stay safe online
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Millions of teenagers use social media every day, and most of them have a great time. [1] However, there are a few simple rules that can help you avoid problems.

First, choose strong passwords. A good password has at least twelve letters and includes numbers. [2] Never use the same password for different accounts, because if one is stolen, all the others are in danger.

Second, think carefully before you share a photograph. [3] Once a picture is online, you cannot control who sees it or where it goes. Ask yourself whether you would be happy for your teacher or your grandmother to look at it.

Third, be careful about meeting people that you only know online. [4] If you do decide to meet someone, take a friend with you and choose a public place. Finally, remember that you can always talk to an adult if something makes you feel uncomfortable. [5] They will not be angry, and they might be able to help.
sentences: Photos can stay on the internet for years.
Many adults forget their passwords too.
The internet can be a wonderful place to make friends and learn new things.
Using your pet's name is not a good idea.
Parents and teachers usually understand more than you expect.
Not everyone is honest about who they are.

gaps.explanation: "Have a great time" is followed by the positive description, and "However" introduces the rules.
A good password is described, and a pet's name is an example of what to avoid.
"Once a picture is online" explains why photos stay on the internet for a long time.
Not everyone is honest explains why meeting online friends is risky.
"They" refers to parents and teachers, who will not be angry.

turns.text: Welcome to our Computer Club, everyone. We meet every Thursday after school, from four o'clock until half past five. This term, we're going to learn how to build a simple website. parts.title: A teenage video-maker
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: concetta
turns.text: Today I'm talking to Kasimir Brandt, who is seventeen and makes videos. Kasimir, what were your first videos about?

turns.speaker: kasimir
turns.text: Skateboarding. I was thirteen, and I filmed my friends doing tricks. The pictures were shaky, but people seemed to enjoy them.

turns.speaker: concetta
turns.text: How many people follow your channel now?

turns.speaker: kasimir
turns.text: About two thousand. It isn't a huge number, but I know many of them by name because they write to me.

turns.speaker: concetta
turns.text: Do you ever get unkind comments?

turns.speaker: kasimir
turns.text: Sometimes. At the beginning, they made me feel terrible. Now I just ignore them. Arguing only makes things worse.

turns.speaker: concetta
turns.text: Do you follow any safety rules?

turns.speaker: kasimir
turns.text: Yes, the most important one is never to show where I live. I always check the background of a video before I post it.

turns.speaker: concetta
turns.text: How do you find time for school?

turns.speaker: kasimir
turns.text: I only film at weekends. During the week, homework comes first, and my mother makes sure that I stick to that.

turns.speaker: concetta
turns.text: What would you like to do in the future?

turns.speaker: kasimir
turns.text: I'd like to study film-making at university, and perhaps make documentaries one day.
